---
title: Observation weighting
---

#### Purpose

Inspect every variable assigned the **Weighting** role and the effective weight obtained by multiplying them. Optionally change the shape of a component or the effective distribution, and configure importance-only or uniform Test weighting. The card has no flip side.

#### Reading the front

Normal view shows only effective-weight bars and a horizontal effective-distribution chart. Full screen adds a top row of equally sized component bar charts when there are two or more Weighting variables. All components share that top row. The effective bar chart and distribution remain together below, sharing a Y scale with a narrow gap and a 70:30 width split. With a single Weighting variable, both views show the same two charts. Scroll vertically in full screen when more panels are needed.

Observation bars have **Observations** on the horizontal axis and **Weights** on the vertical axis. Observation numbers are one-based positions in the current input, not unique identifiers. The display limit thins bars at evenly spaced positions without changing the data. The distribution has **Counts** on the horizontal axis and **Weights** on the vertical axis; it counts every observation, including zero weights.

The footer reports:

* The number and proportion of observations with zero effective weight.
* Effective sample size, $(\sum w)^2/\sum w^2$, as a concentration diagnostic rather than a claim about independent observations.
* The largest observation's fraction of total weight.

More than 10% zero effective weights is flagged. Such weights remain visible here for investigation, but downstream statistical cards fall back to unweighted calculations and explain this in Settings. Exactly 10% is allowed. An all-zero distribution has effective sample size zero. Missing, negative, nonnumeric or infinite components produce an explanation instead of a misleading plot.

#### Shape buttons and component selection

The footer buttons apply immediately to downstream data:

| Button | Power | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| Square | 2 | Increase relative extremes. |
| Original | 1 | Restore this card's incoming component values. |
| Square root | 0.5 | Reduce relative extremes. |
| Cube root | 1/3 | Reduce relative extremes more strongly. |

Choose **Component to transform** in settings. **Effective (all components)** applies the same power to each component, making the resulting product proportional to the original product raised to that power. Alternatively select one component to alter only that contribution. Component names and roles are preserved; `balance__` continues to identify balancing factors.

For a selected component, the transformation is

$$w'_i = w_i^p\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathrm{Train}}w_j}{\sum_{j\in\mathrm{Train}}w_j^p}.$$

The implementation rescales the calculation for numerical stability. Each component retains its training mean; the **total effective product need not be preserved** when several components are changed. All-zero components remain zero. Positive powers preserve zeros: these buttons cannot repair a large zero-weight fraction.

This is a nonnegative power transformation, not ordinary Box–Cox. [The Box–Cox formula](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.boxcox.html) subtracts one and divides by the power (or takes a logarithm), so it can produce negative weights and has restrictions at zero. Here powers are deliberately positive and the output stays nonnegative.

#### What is a good distribution?

There is no universally desirable shape and no requirement for normally distributed weights. Uniform weights maximize the concentration-based effective sample size for a fixed row count, but may discard intended importance or balancing information. A distribution dominated by a few observations, a small effective sample size, or many zeros warrants investigation; none alone establishes that the weighting is wrong.

First check which component causes the concentration and why it exists. Transform a particular component when that contribution is the concern. Transform the effective distribution when the combined importance is intentionally being moderated. Changing balancing factors can undo equal class-weight totals; changing importance weights changes the learning and scoring objective. Compare downstream performance using the intended evaluation policy rather than choosing the smoothest-looking histogram.

#### Training, Test and persistence

The chart is an **all-data Training preview**. A saved, unfitted pipeline step learns each normalization constant afresh from its training fold. Future transformations reuse those constants and never normalize on Test data. Missing training-only `balance__` columns are skipped during inference; required selected importance columns must still exist.

**Test weighting** is saved in the pipeline:

* **Importance only** multiplies Weighting components whose names do not start with `balance__`.
* **Uniform (no weights)** ignores every component.

The latest observation-weighting step supplies the default policy when `Card.effective_weights(data, purpose="test")` is called on its downstream proxy data. An explicit `test_policy` argument overrides it. A fitted step also exposes `evaluation_weights(transformed_frame)` for already-transformed Test rows. The evaluator must request and pass these weights to its scoring method; storing a policy does not automatically route `sample_weight` into an arbitrary estimator.

**Preview Test weighting** illustrates the policy on the current observations. It does not create a holdout or refit on Test observations. Display limits, bins, and the Test-preview switch do not affect exported data. Power, component, and policy selections are bookmarkable. Original resets this card's transformation while keeping its Test-policy setting.
